terms.definition: Descriptive term from witnesses; coined by media covering Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting. Used matter-of-factly in government documents.
Plural form used extensively in FBI and Air Force correspondence.
Military-preferred term in late 1940s, considered more neutral than 'saucer'.
Plural form common in Army Air Forces and early Air Force communications.
Coined by USAF Captain Edward Ruppelt to replace loaded 'flying saucer'. Became the standard term for decades.
Unidentified Aerial Phenomena / Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena. Current official US government designation, replacing UFO to remove cultural stigma and broaden scope.
Generic term used in academic and official contexts to avoid the baggage of 'UFO'.
Military operational term for unidentified objects that intrude into restricted airspace or testing ranges. Threat-neutral framing — the object is just 'in the way'.
Standard military aviation term for an unidentified radar contact. No UFO-specific connotation.
Calling it a 'craft' implies it's a manufactured vehicle — subtly assumes intelligent construction rather than natural phenomenon.
Implies extraterrestrial origin. Used in NASA documents for known vehicles but loaded when applied to UAP.
Community-preferred term for spherical luminous UAP. Carries connotations of the paranormal.
Plural. Often associated with formations of luminous objects.
Plural. Documented by multiple Allied air crews over both European and Pacific theaters.
Specific phenomenon observed near nuclear installations in New Mexico. Subject of Project Twinkle.
Plural. Concentrated over Los Alamos and Sandia nuclear facilities.
Pentagon term expanding UAP beyond just 'aerial' to include underwater and space observations.
Shape descriptor from the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter, now a community shorthand for that specific case. Using it signals familiarity with modern UAP lore.
Hyphenated variant of the Nimitz case descriptor.
Term for rocket-shaped objects seen over Scandinavia in 1946. Initially attributed to Soviet missile tests.
Generic descriptor for bright luminous objects. Can be mundane (meteor) or anomalous depending on context.
Plural form common in Air Force incident summaries.
The 'default' theory — visitors from another planet. Present in original documents but always as hypothesis, never conclusion.
In government docs often means simply 'foreign'. In community usage assumes non-human origin.
Generic term used in FBI case files when discussing the extraterrestrial hypothesis.
1950s-era term for the ET hypothesis. Appears in both original FBI surveillance of contactees and Air Force memos.
Updated version of 'interplanetary' — from other star systems rather than just other planets.
1950s contactee terminology. Appears heavily in FBI surveillance of the Amalgamated Flying Saucer Clubs.
Contactee-era term implying benevolent ET visitors. Signals the 1950s Space Age utopian worldview.
Plain-language version of the ET hypothesis found in early government documents and witness statements.
Hypothesis that UAP originate from parallel dimensions. Using this term signals rejection of simple ET explanation and alignment with Vallee's framework.
John Keel's term for non-human intelligence that is native to Earth but operates in dimensions beyond normal perception. A tribal marker — using it identifies you as deep in UAP theory.
Hidden Earth-based civilization hypothesis. Gained academic attention from a 2024 Harvard paper. Using it signals awareness of cutting-edge UAP theory beyond mainstream.
The deliberately agnostic term from 2023 congressional language. Avoids specifying ET vs interdimensional vs cryptoterrestrial. Sounds neutral but presupposes intelligence.
Shorthand for non-human intelligence. The term from the 2023 UAP Disclosure Act.
Single-word variant appearing in some government documents.
Theory that Earth contains habitable interior spaces. Appears in FBI files via Dr. Raymond Bernard's book sold through contactee clubs. The concept behind 'Agartha'.
Legendary lost civilization. Single mention in FBI case file. Signals esoteric/ancient-mystery worldview.
Hypothetical lost continent. Single mention in FBI case file. Deep esoteric territory.
Short for 'breakaway civilization' — the idea that a secret human group has developed vastly superior technology.
Joseph Farrell's hypothesis that post-WWII black projects created a secret technologically advanced society. Using the full phrase is a strong community identifier.
Religious interpretation framework. Rare in this corpus — appears in FBI contactee surveillance.
Generic term for entities. In FBI files, used by contactees describing their claimed encounters.
The archetypical alien entity type with large eyes and grey skin. Dominates post-1980s abduction accounts. Note: in early docs often just a color descriptor.
Clinical term used in official reports for entities observed in or near UAP. Implies a vehicle with pilots.
Neutral descriptor. Used in FBI files when agents document witness claims.
Scientific framing. In FBI files, used in context of physical evidence collection.
Descriptive term meaning human-shaped. Used in official reports without implying specific alien typology.
David Grusch's term from 2023 congressional testimony — 'non-human biologics'. Using this word in UAP context immediately references his claims.
Person claiming ongoing contact with extraterrestrial beings. The 1950s contactee movement is extensively documented in FBI surveillance files.
Plural. The FBI monitored contactee organizations as potential subversive groups.
Clinical term. Less loaded than 'beings' as it doesn't presuppose biological nature.
The most commonly reported UAP shape across all eras and agencies.
Surface descriptor. Implies manufactured rather than natural object.
Round/spherical shape. Second most common after disc.
Adjective form of sphere descriptor.
Elongated cylindrical shape. Common in 1950s-60s reports, sometimes called 'mother ships' in community lore.
Triangle-shaped objects became prominent in the 1980s-90s. Community often links these to alleged 'TR-3B' black project aircraft.
See triangular. The Belgium wave of 1989-90 made triangles a dominant UAP archetype.
Emitting light. Straightforward observational descriptor.
Light-emitting. Plain-language descriptor.
Cylinder-shaped. Technical variant of 'cigar-shaped'.
Light that pulses or throbs. In community lore, pulsating lights are considered a hallmark of 'genuine' UAP vs conventional aircraft.
Stationary flight. The most commonly reported UAP behavior across all document types.
Multiple objects maintaining spatial relationships. Can imply coordination/intelligence.
Directed movement changes. Standard military observational language.
Object appears to deliberately avoid pursuit or detection. Implies intelligence and awareness of the observer.
Rapid speed changes. When described as 'extreme' or 'instantaneous', implies technology beyond known capability.
Moving between air, water, and space without observable transition. Pentagon-coined term that implies capabilities beyond any known technology.
Becoming invisible or radar-transparent. Borrows from science fiction; implies advanced stealth technology.
Matching speed and course of an aircraft. Strongly implies awareness and intent.

Lue Elizondo's framework: instantaneous acceleration, hypersonic velocity, low observability, transmedium travel, positive lift without propulsion. Using this term signals alignment with AATIP's analytical framework.
Primary detection method in military UAP encounters. Radar confirmation elevates a sighting from anecdotal to instrumental.
Signals intelligence. Indicates electronic emissions were detected from the UAP — implies the object has electronic systems.
Geiger counter / radiation detection. Indicates radioactivity was checked at UAP sites. Common in 1940s-50s cases near nuclear installations.
Ionizing radiation detected at UAP encounter sites. In FBI/DoW docs, systematic radiation checks were standard protocol.
EM effects — vehicle stalling, radio interference, compass deviation. One of the most consistently reported physical effects.
Active interference with radar systems. Implies electronic warfare capability.
Camera/imaging systems. Modern military UAP reports increasingly rely on EO/IR sensor data.
Forward-Looking Infrared. The sensor type that captured the famous Nimitz/Gimbal/GoFast videos.
All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. Current Pentagon office for UAP investigation. Replaced UAPTF.
USAF program that investigated UFOs 1952-1969. Officially concluded most sightings were explainable; 701 remained 'unidentified'.
Department of War UAP reporting and tracking program referenced in the DoW mission reports in this corpus.
Military program to photograph green fireballs near nuclear installations. Inconclusive results.
Alleged long-running secret UAP reverse-engineering programs. David Grusch's central claim. Using this term presupposes these programs exist.
Plural form. Implies multiple compartmented programs across agencies and contractors.
Alleged secret committee (MJ-12/Majestic-12) established by Truman to manage UAP crash retrievals. Documents widely considered fabricated.
Alleged classified UAP tracking program revealed in 2024 whistleblower complaint. Unconfirmed.
The central community concept — that governments possess UAP truth and the goal is to make them release it. The word itself presupposes there's something to disclose.
Standard government security designation. Factual, not conspiratorial.
Officially released from classification. These documents exist because of declassification.
Plural. This corpus documents extensive redaction patterns across agencies.
Freedom of Information Act. The legal mechanism through which many of these documents were obtained.
Organized concealment. In FBI files appears in context of investigating whether saucer groups pose a subversive threat.
Explicit accusation of organized concealment. Strong claim that presupposes hidden truth.
Deliberate spreading of false information. In UAP context, the accusation that the government actively muddies the waters.
Activities to prevent espionage. In FBI files, appears in context of whether UAP groups were foreign intelligence fronts.
Actively hidden or prevented from publication. Implies intentional concealment.
In UAP context, the hypothesis that consciousness plays a role in the phenomenon — that UAP interact with or respond to human awareness.
Mind-to-mind communication. Appears in FBI files as claims made by contactees under surveillance. Not endorsed by the documents.
Adjective form. Contactee claims of telepathic contact with space beings.
Relating to alleged mental powers. In FBI files, appears in descriptions of contactee-psychics like Maria Elliott.
Relating to a non-physical plane of existence. In this corpus, some hits are OCR artifacts or astronomical context.
Beyond natural law. Rare in this corpus — appears when FBI agents document fringe claims.
Appearance or materialization. In community usage implies UAP 'manifest' rather than simply arriving.
The 'hitchhiker effect' — paranormal phenomena following researchers home from sites like Skinwalker Ranch. Deep community lore.
J. Allen Hynek's term for cases with absurd, reality-bending details. Now community shorthand for the 'woo' aspects of UAP.
Mysterious figures who allegedly intimidate UAP witnesses. Appears in FBI Section 9 — the FBI documented these claims as part of monitoring the saucer community.
Alleged human-alien genetic hybrid. Deep abduction lore. Single mention in this corpus.
Modern replacement for 'contactee' or 'abductee'. Designed to be less stigmatizing but signals the experiencer community.
How something moves. Neutral engineering term. Becomes loaded when paired with 'exotic' or 'unknown'.
Propulsion via gravity manipulation. Not recognized by mainstream physics. Appears in FBI contactee surveillance files.
Single-word variant. Same connotations as anti-gravity.
Energy from nothing — violates thermodynamics. In FBI files, appears in contactee group literature being surveilled.
Recovery of downed UAP. Central to Grusch's 2023 testimony. Using this presupposes that crashes have occurred and materials were recovered.
Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Housed Project Blue Book and the Foreign Technology Division. In UAP lore, alleged storage site for recovered materials.
Socorro, New Mexico. Site of police officer Lonnie Zamora's 1964 close encounter — one of the best-documented cases.
Roswell, New Mexico. The most culturally iconic UAP case. Officially a weather balloon; community insists crash retrieval. The word itself is a litmus test.
One of three Pentagon-released UAP videos (with GoFast and FLIR1). Named after the rotating motion visible in the footage.
J. Allen Hynek, astronomer and Blue Book scientific advisor who evolved from skeptic to advocate. Citing Hynek signals scientific credibility.
Major Donald Keyhoe, Marine Corps aviator who led NICAP. His books appear in FBI surveillance files.
Captain Edward Ruppelt, first head of Project Blue Book. Coined the term 'UFO'.
Richard Doty, AFOSI agent accused of running disinformation against UFO researchers. Citing Doty signals awareness of the government disinfo narrative.
Jacques Vallee, astronomer/computer scientist who proposed the interdimensional hypothesis. Citing Vallee signals openness to non-ET explanations.
Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense. Key figure in getting the Pentagon UAP videos released.
Sean Kirkpatrick, first director of AARO. Controversial in community for dismissive conclusions.
National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena. Serious civilian research org that fought for disclosure.
Government oversight role. In UAP context, the Intelligence Community IG validated Grusch's complaint as 'credible and urgent'.
Relating to Congress. UAP hearings in 2023-2024 were watershed moments.
The UAP Disclosure Act included eminent domain provisions for recovered materials. This specific term signals deep knowledge of the legislation.
